1212.title: Perfect joy (Little Flowers 8)
1212.hook: Francis says perfect joy is being turned away in the cold and staying patient
1212.howItsDone: Franciscan friars, sisters and lay Franciscans read the story of perfect joy from the Little Flowers, and some return to it when they meet rejection or hardship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lady Poverty: Francis going without, for love. Your line was poor for love.

Winter, on a road in Umbria. Two friars are walking home to their little church, Saint Mary of the Angels: Francis, and Brother Leo a little way ahead. It is bitterly cold. Every so often Francis calls out. Brother Leo, write this down: if the friars everywhere gave a great example of holiness, that is not perfect joy. If a friar could heal the sick and make the blind see, not perfect joy. If he knew every language and every science, not perfect joy. If he preached so well that whole peoples came to faith, still not. Until Leo asks: then, Father, for God's sake, where is perfect joy?
screen: `A ROAD IN WINTER.` → `NOT MIRACLES. NOT LEARNING.` → `THEN WHERE IS PERFECT JOY?`

segments.voice: The story comes from the Little Flowers of Saint Francis. Here is his answer. When we reach Saint Mary of the Angels, soaked with rain, stiff with cold, muddy and hungry, we knock at the gate. The porter comes out angry and asks who we are. Two of your brothers, we say. And he says, you're lying, you're a pair of tramps who go around stealing alms from the poor. He won't open, and leaves us out in the snow and the rain until night. If we bear that patiently, without grumbling, and think humbly that perhaps the porter knows us better than we know ourselves, Brother Leo, write that this is perfect joy. Francis pushes further: if the porter comes back with a knotted stick, and we bear that too, thinking of what Christ suffered, there is perfect joy. Then he explains. Everything on his list, the miracles, the learning, the preaching, is a gift from God, so there's nothing in it to boast about. He quotes Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "what hast thou that thou hast not received?" The one thing we can offer of our own is to bear a hardship for love of Christ. And he closes with Paul again: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Francis isn't saying the porter is right, or that cruelty is good. He's pulling joy apart from success and recognition. The joy he means is the kind a locked gate can't take away.
screen: `SOAKED, FROZEN, TURNED AWAY.` · `BEAR IT PATIENTLY: PERFECT JOY.` · `EVERY GIFT WAS RECEIVED.` · `A JOY A LOCKED GATE CAN'T TAKE.` · then, large: `WHAT HAST THOU THAT THOU HAST NOT RECEIVED?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a recent no, a request turned down, and stand outside that door again for a moment, noticing whatever rises. You don't have to push it away; just breathe beside it, the way Francis pictures standing in the snow, and let your shoulders drop. If you pray, offer that closed door to God; if not, just rest outside the gate.
Perfect joy. For Francis, not success or praise, but patience outside a closed gate, for love of Christ. Today's word.
Your line: perfect joy. Every gift on Francis's list was received; the patience was his to give. Rest well.

1213.title: The wolf of Gubbio (Little Flowers 21)
1213.hook: a legend of Francis making peace between a wolf and a town
1213.howItsDone: The wolf of Gubbio is one of the stories told about Francis in the Little Flowers, and Catholics, especially Franciscans, retell it in sermons, art and children's books as a story of peacemaking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, perfect joy: patience outside a locked gate, for love of Christ. Your line was perfect joy.

The town of Gubbio has stopped going outside. A wolf, huge and fierce, has been killing animals in the fields, and people too. Anyone who leaves the walls goes armed, as if heading into battle, and plenty don't leave at all. Into this town walks a small man in a patched habit. He hears about the wolf, and says he's going out to meet it. The people beg him not to. He makes the sign of the cross and walks out anyway, the townspeople climbing wherever they can to watch. Today, a legend from the Little Flowers.
screen: `A TOWN AFRAID TO GO OUT.` → `A SMALL MAN WALKS TOWARD IT.` → `HE WALKS OUT ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: The wolf charges. Francis makes the sign of the cross over it and calls it by a family name: Brother Wolf. Come here, he says, and in the name of Christ, do no harm to me or to anyone. In the story the wolf closes its mouth, slows, and lies down at his feet like a lamb. Then he talks to it straight: you've done great harm. You've killed God's creatures, and people made in God's image, and the whole town is against you. But I want to make peace between you and them. Here's the turn: Francis has noticed why the wolf kills. It's hungry. So the peace has two sides. The wolf will harm no one, and the town will feed it for as long as it lives, so hunger never drives it to harm anyone again. Francis asks for a pledge and holds out his hand, and the wolf lays its paw in his palm. In the town square, in front of everyone, the bargain is made again, paw and all. After that, the story says, the wolf went from door to door, the people fed it kindly, and no dog barked at it. People read the legend in more than one way. Some read a real animal and a real wonder; some, a picture of a town and its enemy, a fierce man perhaps. Either way, Francis doesn't kill the wolf or chase it off. He gives it a brother's name, and asks what it needs.

segments.voice: Bring to mind something prowling around the edges of your life, a conversation you dread, a worry about someone you love, and let it come near, the way the wolf came near, without running at it or from it. Then ask it Francis's question: what does this fear actually want, maybe safety, an answer, to be taken seriously? If you pray, make the sign of the cross and hold it before God; if not, breathe with it at arm's length.

Your line: brother wolf. The peace had two sides, and the town kept its half. Until tomorrow.

1214.title: The birds
1214.hook: Francis preaches to the birds, who stay to listen
1214.howItsDone: Catholics remember Francis's sermon to the birds in art and story, and on or near his feast day some parishes hold a blessing of animals in his honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wolf of Gubbio: a peace where the town fed its old enemy. Your line was brother wolf.

What would you say to a flock of birds, if you thought they were listening? Shoo, maybe. Francis is on the road with his companions in the Umbrian countryside when he sees trees by the way filled with birds, and more on the ground. He tells his brothers to wait and walks over, alone, into the middle of them. They don't scatter. The ones in the trees come down and gather at his feet, waiting. He has an audience, so he preaches.
screen: `TREES FULL OF BIRDS.` → `THEY DON'T SCATTER.` → `SO HE PREACHES.`

segments.voice: Thomas of Celano, an early biographer, tells this story, and so do the Little Flowers. Francis begins the way he begins with anyone: my little sisters the birds. His sermon isn't a scolding. It's a list of gifts. You owe a great deal to God your Creator, he tells them, so praise him always. He gave you freedom to fly anywhere, and clothing, feathers twice and three times over. He kept your kind safe in Noah's ark. He gave you the air, springs and rivers to drink from, mountains and valleys for shelter, tall trees for your nests. And you don't sow or reap, and God feeds you anyway. That last line is Jesus's own, from the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the birds of the air, for they neither sow, nor do they reap, nor gather into barns." Francis is reading the gospel back to the ones it was about. The Little Flowers says they open their beaks, stretch out their necks, spread their wings and bow their heads to the ground, as if to show they understood. They don't leave until he blesses them with the sign of the cross. Then they rise all at once, singing, and fly off north, south, east and west, so the flock makes a cross in the sky. Celano adds a human detail. Francis blamed himself for never having preached to birds before, and from then on, the story says, urged every creature he met to praise its Maker. In his eyes the whole creation was singing, and he'd been slow to join in.
screen: `MY LITTLE SISTERS THE BIRDS.` · `A SERMON THAT'S A LIST OF GIFTS.` · `THEY BOW, THEN FLY OFF IN A CROSS.` · `HE BLAMED HIMSELF FOR BEING LATE.` · then, large: `BEHOLD THE BIRDS OF THE AIR.`

segments.voice: Open a window if you can, and listen outward, past the hum of the house and the traffic, and wait for a bird. When one comes, don't name it; just hear it the way Francis heard his audience, something alive making its own sound, and if none comes, any living sound will do. If you pray, let that sound be a small praise you join; if you don't, let it be company.

1215.title: Clare's sisters
1215.hook: enclosed, poor and joyful, praying for the world
1215.howItsDone: Poor Clare monasteries live in enclosure and pray the Liturgy of the Hours through the day, and some Catholics send them prayer requests by letter or leave them at the monastery door.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birds: Francis's sermon to his little sisters. Your line was sisters birds.

Night in Assisi. A young woman from a noble family slips out of her father's house, by a side door, tradition says, and hurries down the hill to the little church where Francis and his brothers live. They meet her with torches. There, before the altar, she lays aside her fine clothes, and Francis cuts off her hair. Her name is Clare, and this path met her early on. Soon after, at the convent where Francis has sent her, her family comes to bring her home, and she holds on to the altar and won't let go. Today, the women who followed her, and the hidden life they chose.
screen: `A DOOR OPENS AT NIGHT.` → `TORCHES, AND HER HAIR CUT.` → `SHE WON'T GO HOME.`

segments.voice: Clare settles at San Damiano, the small church Francis had rebuilt with his own hands. Other women join her, her own sister among them, and they become the Poor Ladies, known today as the Poor Clares. Their life has three marks. The first is poverty, and Clare holds on to it fiercely. Her early biography says a pope once offered to free her from her vow of poverty, so the sisters could own property and be secure. She told him she never wanted to be freed from following Christ. What she asked for instead was a privilege: the right to own nothing at all. The second mark is enclosure. The sisters stay inside the monastery walls; visitors speak to them through a grille, and the world mostly goes on without seeing them. To an outside eye that can look like hiding. Clare saw it as making room. Jesus says in the gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, "enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret." The enclosure is a whole life lived behind that shut door. The third mark is one an outsider might not expect: joy. Clare's letters to Agnes of Prague, a princess who chose the same life, are full of it. She tells Agnes to gaze into Christ as into a mirror, every day, and to see herself there. And Poor Clares pray for the world outside, for people who'll never know their names. Hidden, in their tradition, doesn't mean absent. It means close by, unseen, holding things up.
screen: `POVERTY: THE PRIVILEGE OF OWNING NOTHING.` · `ENCLOSURE: BEHIND THE SHUT DOOR.` · `JOY: CHRIST AS A MIRROR.` · `PRAYING FOR A WORLD THAT DOESN'T SEE.` · then, large: `PRAY TO THY FATHER IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Somewhere right now, behind a wall you'll never walk through, sisters are at prayer; you don't know their names, and they don't know yours. Hold them in mind, and anyone who quietly keeps others in prayer. If you pray, pray for them; if you don't, send them your thanks into the quiet.

1216.title: The Third Order
1216.hook: laypeople who follow Francis in family and work
1216.howItsDone: Secular Franciscans are lay Catholics, single or married, who make a profession to live the gospel in the spirit of Francis, meet regularly in local fraternities, and carry that life into their families and work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Poor Clares: poor, enclosed, glad, praying for a world that rarely sees them. Your line was hidden prayer.

A preacher has just finished, and the whole town wants to go with him. That's the scene in the Little Flowers, in a village near Assisi called Cannara, the same chapter that tells of the birds. Francis preaches, and the people are so moved that men and women alike want to leave their houses, their fields, their families, and follow him on the road. On paper, a preacher's dream. But Francis says no. Don't be in a hurry, he tells them. Don't leave. I'll arrange what you should do. There are the brothers, and Clare's sisters. What about everyone else?
screen: `A WHOLE TOWN WANTS TO FOLLOW.` → `DON'T BE IN A HURRY.` → `WHAT ABOUT EVERYONE ELSE?`

segments.voice: The Little Flowers says that after Cannara, Francis began to think about a third order, for people who would follow him without leaving home. Married people. Parents. Farmers, merchants, workers. In the early days they were called the brothers and sisters of penance, and penance there doesn't mean misery. It means turning, a whole life turned toward God. Today the Church calls it the Secular Franciscan Order, secular meaning lived in the world, not in a cloister. Francis wrote a letter to people like this, to all the faithful living in the world. In it he says, more or less: love God with your whole heart, love your neighbor as yourself, turn from what pulls you away, receive the Body and Blood of the Lord. Then something startling. People who live like that, he writes, are the spouses and brothers and mothers of Jesus Christ. He's leaning on the gospel, where Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "whosoever shall do the will of my Father, that is in heaven, he is my brother, and my sister, and my mother." Not a monk. Not a friar. Anyone. You don't need a habit or a monastery to belong to Francis's family. The poverty looks different at home: a simpler house, a lighter grip on things, generosity with time. The peace looks different: a kitchen table, an office, a difficult relative. Secular Franciscans make a promise, meet in local groups, and go back to their lives. The point was never to run away from ordinary life. It was to bring Francis into it.

If you pray, ask Francis's God for help to keep it; if not, just hold the picture steady.

1217.title: Anthony and the fish
1217.hook: a legend: when no one listens, Anthony preaches to the fish
1217.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Anthony of Padua as a Franciscan preacher, and his sermon to the fish is a favorite subject in Franciscan art and storytelling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Third Order: laypeople following Francis without leaving home. Your line was francis at home.

A friar has walked into Rimini, a city on the sea, to preach, and nobody will listen. The Little Flowers says people there had turned against the Church's teaching, and they won't come to hear him. The friar is Anthony, later known as Anthony of Padua, the finder of lost things this path met on his feast day. The obvious next move: leave. Shake the dust off. Instead, Anthony walks down to where the river meets the sea, stands on the bank, and starts preaching to the water.
screen: `A CITY THAT WON'T LISTEN.` → `ANTHONY OF PADUA.` → `HE PREACHES TO THE WATER.`

segments.voice: He calls out: hear the word of God, you fishes of the sea and of the river, since the people won't. And in the legend they come. So many fish gather that the water fills with them, all with their heads above the surface, all facing him, and in order: the little ones near the shore, the middle-sized behind them, the big ones out in the deep. Then, like Francis with the birds, he counts out what God has given them. Water, fresh and salt. Places to shelter from storms, and food. When the flood came and the animals outside the ark perished, you were kept alive. God chose a fish to carry the prophet Jonah and set him safe on land. A fish brought up the coin that Peter paid as tax. And after he rose, Christ himself ate fish. At this, the story says, the fish open their mouths and bow their heads, as if to praise. Word gets around. People come running down to the river, and the ones who had refused to listen come too. They're moved, they fall at Anthony's feet, and now he preaches to them. That's the happy ending, but notice the order. Anthony doesn't preach to the fish as a trick to win the crowd back. Nothing in the story says he expected anyone to come. He preached because preaching was his work, and the fish were who was there. Paul tells Timothy, in the Douay-Rheims: "Preach the word: be instant in season, out of season." In season is when they're listening. Out of season is the riverbank.

1218.title: Bonaventure's mind
1218.hook: the Franciscan way of thinking: love goes further than knowledge
1218.howItsDone: Franciscans and other Catholics read Bonaventure's Journey of the Mind into God as a guide to prayer, and the Church honors him as a saint and a Doctor of the Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anthony and the fish: a preacher refused by a city, preaching to the water. Your line was preach anyway.

Francis never wrote a book of theology. He told his brothers to work with their hands, to preach peace, to bear a locked gate patiently. Then the brotherhood grows, and some of the friars end up in lecture halls. One of them teaches at the university of Paris, in a world of disputations, where a question is argued for and against, point by point. So what does a friar like that do with a founder who preached to birds? Does he leave the stories behind? Today, the scholar who tried to think the Franciscan way.
screen: `A FOUNDER WHO WROTE NO THEOLOGY.` → `A FRIAR IN A LECTURE HALL.` → `DOES HE LEAVE THE STORIES?`

segments.voice: His name is Bonaventure. He taught in Paris, he led the Franciscan order, and he wrote a life of Francis. He also wrote a short book with a long name, The Journey of the Mind into God, which this path has walked once before. He went up to La Verna, the mountain where Francis had seen a vision of a seraph, an angel with six wings, and there, looking for peace, he came to see the six wings as six steps of a journey toward God. First you find God's traces in the world outside: in stones, plants, birds, everything that is. Then you turn inward and find God's image in your own mind, in memory, understanding and love. Then you look above the mind, to God himself. It's a ladder of thought, and hard going. But before you set out, Bonaventure warns: don't think reading is enough without the anointing of grace, or thinking without devotion, or study without wonder, or knowledge without love. And at the top of the ladder he tells the mind to let go of its thinking. If you want to know how this happens, ask grace, not learning. Ask desire, not understanding. Ask the groaning of prayer, not the diligence of study. Ask the Bridegroom, not the teacher. Paul says it to the Corinthians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Knowledge puffeth up; but charity edifieth." Bonaventure didn't throw away knowledge; he spent his life teaching and writing. But in this book knowledge reaches an edge, and love keeps going. Think as hard as you can, then let love carry you the rest of the way.
screen: `SIX WINGS, SIX STEPS TO GOD.` · `OUTSIDE, INSIDE, ABOVE.` · `ASK GRACE, NOT LEARNING.` · `KNOWLEDGE STOPS; LOVE KEEPS GOING.` · then, large: `KNOWLEDGE PUFFETH UP; BUT CHARITY EDIFIETH.`
